cim: Circular Finance May Set Up Systemic Risk in Artificial Intelligence
cim_eredeti: Circular Finance May Set Up Systemic Risk in Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Financial arrangements in which artificial intelligence companies invest in businesses that then purchase their products or services could expose the broader economy to financial instability, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. ​

The practice, known as circular financing, has become increasingly prominent as technology companies pour billions of dollars into AI infrastructure. Analysts estimate U.S. AI-related infrastructure investment at approximately $500 billion this year and $10.3 trillion between 2025 and 2032, according to CRS.

The arrangements are raising questions for Congress about whether the AI industry's rapid expansion could create economic or financial shocks and whether circular financing could amplify those disruptions. The report stops short of concluding that an AI investment bubble exists or that circular financing would necessarily trigger a broader financial crisis.

Circular financing occurs when a company provides financial support to another business with the expectation that the recipient will purchase its products or services. The arrangements have become increasingly common among AI developers, chipmakers and cloud computing providers. The Bank for International Settlements found that 28.7% of investments made by AI companies between 2021 and 2025, measured by deal value, went to other AI companies. It also found that 55.2% of investment flowing into AI companies came from other AI businesses.

The report identifies three types of circular financing arrangements: investor-supplier relationships, in which a company finances a customer's purchase of its products; investor-purchaser relationships, in which a customer invests in its supplier; and reciprocal arrangements involving financial commitments between companies. One prominent example involves Nvidia and OpenAI. On Sept. 22, 2025, Nvidia announced that it intended to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI as the companies developed computing infrastructure powered by Nvidia technology.

However, Reuters reported in January, citing The Wall Street Journal, that the investment plan had stalled, raising questions about whether the proposed financing would proceed. Another example involves Amazon and Anthropic. In April, Amazon announced an additional $5 billion investment in the AI developer, with the potential for another $20 billion. Anthropic also committed to spending $100 billion over 10 years on Amazon's chips and cloud computing services.

The report describes these arrangements as expanded forms of vendor financing, a longstanding practice in which suppliers help customers finance purchases. Such deals can provide companies with capital they might otherwise struggle to obtain, while suppliers may be better positioned than traditional lenders to assess their customers' risks.

The financing is particularly important for leading AI developers, many of which are startups spending more money than they generate in revenue and relying on outside investment to expand their operations. However, the arrangements can also make it more difficult for investors to determine whether demand for AI products and computing infrastructure reflects genuine market growth or spending supported by the companies supplying those products.

The report warns that complex financial agreements may obscure how much AI companies depend on one another, potentially understating their exposure to financial problems elsewhere in the industry. The report compares these dynamics to earlier technology investment booms, including circular financing relationships between telecommunications equipment suppliers and customers during the dot-com era. When investment dried up, companies that depended on continued financing struggled to survive, and some ultimately failed.

The growing financial ties among AI companies could let problems at one business spread to its suppliers, investors, and customers. If major banks or other financial institutions become heavily exposed to those arrangements, disruptions in the AI industry could also affect broader financial markets.

The International Monetary Fund's October Global Financial Stability Report identified a potential correction in AI-related investment as a major concern among financial market participants. However, the extent of the risk depends partly on how companies finance their investments. When businesses fund AI investments through their own operating revenue rather than borrowing from banks or other financial institutions, the financial system's immediate exposure may be more limited.

For Congress, the unresolved question is whether circular financing primarily helps companies build the infrastructure needed for AI development or creates financial dependencies that could deepen the consequences of an industry downturn.
